If you are building a startup, try to be profitable when you are small.

Focus on product led growth.
Built clear edge with product.

100% work from office, it helps.
Extremely low marketing spends.
Focus on unit economics, from day 1.

When you scale a startup and become large with zero profits, it becomes extremely difficult to turn things around. Not impossible, but is super challenging.

Scale now, profitable later works very rarely.

Your coding agent is making product decisions you didn't know you were delegating.

After it builds a feature, try this:

"Compare my requests with the current implementation. Find up to three consequential user-facing choices I didn't specify. Show the evidence for each. If context is missing, say so. Don't change anything."

Try it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Lovable, or Replit. Use the same project so it can see your original requests.

The agent may have decided whether someone can skip signup or what happens when a customer cancels.

Your users won't know the agent made those choices. They'll just live with them.

Josh Gruenstein of Tutor Intelligence says he watched robot startups die the same way "5 to 10 times in a row," and explains what they got wrong:

"We started this company at a time we're seeing all of these very academic supply chain oriented robotic startups get started and then not succeed... One of the big things I think that robotics companies get wrong is they're not actually product companies."

"They're like, 'Okay, some really big company has a very specific problem... We're gonna spend two years building a very custom system to solve their problem.'"

"Chances are it won't work... doing product requires iteration. Even if it does work, who's to say that customer still has that problem? So boom, the company's done."

"Working with a diverse range of customers is this beautiful forcing function for building the right shape of product, which to us is a general robot."

"If you can sign a contract in two weeks with a mid-market customer and have a robot running immediately after that... you know you're being successful."

candidates.text:
I just hung up from a 26 minute call that was supposed to be 90 seconds.

An AI founder opted in on my funnel and I called to see if he was a fit.

Two minutes in, he opened up.

He had spent the last 12 months building four products: a GPU service, a social network, an AI scheduling tool and AI agents infra.

Then he said this:

"I've been building for so long but I have no users and I know nothing about marketing."

I asked if he was doing any marketing. He said: "I'm not spending on marketing right now because I have no users."

I stopped him there.

"Is not having users a symptom or the root cause?" I asked him.

"What do you mean?" he asked.

"If you had started marketing six months ago, would you have users today?"

"Potentially, yes." he answered

So no users is the symptom. The root cause is no distribution.

He was waiting for users before investing in marketing. 

But users come from marketing. He was pushing off the very thing that would lead his business growing. 

If you're a founder with something good that nobody uses, more features won't fix it.

People knowing you exist will.

candidates.text:
Let me tell you why founder-led content isn't dead, even with AI writing half the internet.

every week someone says it's over

"everyone can generate posts now. the feed is flooded. nobody reads anymore."

the feed is def flooded...

but look at what it's flooded with:

- posts that summarize other posts
- lists w/ no opinion in them
- lesons that could have come from anyone

when everything sounds the same, the thing that stands out isn't better writing.

it's proof that a real person was there.

that's what founders have that AI doesn't:

1. zoom calls where a customer says something surprising

2. decision that cost them or profit them

3. mistakes they'd never make again

4. opinions their opps are too careful to say

5. numbers from their own business

you can't prompt your way into that stuff

so the flood actually helps the founders who post from real work. the gap between "generated" and "lived" gets more obvious every month.

here's what I'd do if I were a founder right now:

1/ post less, but only from things that happened to you this week

2/ say what you think, not what the industry thinks

3/ use AI to sort and sharpen your notes, not to invent them

4/ show the messy middle, not just the wins

I call this "Effort Marketing"

if you're worried you have nothing interesting to say, you probably have more than you think. 

write down every question a customer asked you this month. that's a quarter of posts nobody else can write.

candidates.text:
I don’t even look at design anymore. I just wrote “do good taste stuff” in a markdown file and gave it to an agent.

It’s currently spending three months in Japan on my behalf.

It visits museums, digs through old magazines, and has life changing conversations with people who make chairs and an 88 year old guy named Torakichi who makes fountain pens. Every night it updates the file so I know what kind of person I am becoming.

Apparently the last three days in Kyoto completely changed how I think about layout. I found out about this "new me" from a notification I got while in a Costco parking lot eating a chicken bake.

There’s a second agent turning these experiences into posts about how important it is to get off the computer and experience the world to become truly inspired. A third agent is deciding which of my friends I’ve outgrown. I get a notification when someone is no longer part of my journey. If you're reading this you're probably on that list.

Yesterday a book arrived in the mail. I liked the cover. I just picked it up and thought it looked nice. It felt good.

My smart home alarm went off and my agent told me to put the book down. According to my agent I shouldn't be wasting my time on X.

But this is the new way of designing. If you're not on board you will get left behind. I love it.

I did my undergrad in data science, and now I’m in my first quarter of a CS master’s, learning C for the first time. That means about 4 hours a week writing C by hand.

At the same time, every side project I build is written with coding agents, and my X feed is full of engineers using agents to ship real products really fast. When the class started, I kept asking myself what the point of hand-writing this stuff was when the world is going crazy with coding agent.

Halfway through the course, I feel like I understand C better than other language I frequently use to ship product with AI. Struggling through problems without AI, and explaining them to other people, is what builds problem-solving and decision-making skills. I think those will matter even more once we’re all orchestrating swarms of agents.

So sometimes when learing it’s worth leaving AI alone for 20 minutes and trying to think it through and explain it to yourself.

The Pixxel confusion stems from the fact that there are two different Indian Pvt Ltd which have similar names:

1. Spacepixxel Technologies Pvt Ltd (2018)
- Incorporated in India on 8 June 2018.
- Ownership: Awais Ahmed (49.95%), Kshitij Khandelwal (49.95%) and Pixxelspace India (0.10%).
- FY25 income: ~₹73 lakh.
- ~31 employees (March 2026 estimate).
- This is the entity that signed the Ministry of Defence's 350th iDEX contract in June 2024 and received another iDEX grant in 2025.

2. Pixxelspace India Pvt Ltd (2019)
- Incorporated on 27 March 2019.
- Ownership: ~99.9999% held by US-incorporated Pixxel Space Technologies Inc.
- FY25 revenue: ~₹39.3 crore.
- ~186 employees (May 2026 estimate).
- This is the entity associated with satellite operations and IN-SPACe authorisations.
- It is also the lead entity in the consortium selected to build India's ₹1,200+ crore Earth-observation constellation.

➡️What does this mean?

Pixxel has an Indian founder-controlled entity as well as a much larger Indian operating entity owned by its Delaware parent.

The 1st co is focused on Indian defence development programmes, while the latter handles more global commercial projects

Caveat: I don't have access to intercompany agreements establishing precisely which entity owns which IP, employs which engineers, or holds particular contractual rights (neither would you)

candidates.text:
A lot of people have grown way too dismissive of other people’s life choices, even when they have nothing to do with their own lives. 

It’s mostly a sign of insecurity to try to convince people who are just minding their own business that your way of life is superior.

Some people will have a great relationship with their parents, some others a neutral one, some others an inexistant one.

Some people will get married to the right partner right away, some others will need several attempts to build a happy marriage, some others will stay alone and eventually be fine with it.

Some people will have kids and be extremely happy, some others will feel like they’ve lost their freedom and become irritable parents, some others will not have kids despite wanting them and it won’t be their fault, some others will choose to not have them and live a happy life nevertheless.

Some people will live their whole lives in their hometown or home country and have a great life, some others will move abroad and be miserable, some others will move abroad and succeed beyond their wildest dreams, and some others who wanted to leave but couldn’t will find reasons to eventually be content with what they have.

Everybody is on a unique and unpredictable journey, and the important heuristic to keep in mind is that if you constantly feel the urge to judge others to feel better about yourself, you have yet to find the right direction in life, and vice versa, if you keep getting lucky without understanding why, that’s fine, it’s just reality telling you to keep going in that direction.

candidates.text:
Exponential growth is the best way to deliver for your investors. Nothing else comes close.

If that fails, every other optimization combined may add 1% of that value - particularly around acquisitions.

When a company doesn't hit escape velocity, some founders go on a personal crusade to return investor capital. 1x is their holy grail.

Somehow they believe that if they return the invested capital, a weight will be lifted off their shoulders, or it will wash away sins. Or that investors will not invest in them again if they don't at least return the invested capital.

To earn the right to ask for investment again, they have to return the capital.

In my opinion, that's just the wrong framework. The best way to return capital would've been to build a large company and deliver a 1000x return.

Returning a few extra dollars is obviously better than returning zero, but that doesn't change the math for investors.

The marginal time value of a returned dollar is quite low and drops drastically if it's not a big exit. It shows bad judgment if you waste precious time for pennies.

Focus your time, resources, and effort on the next big win.

Fighting a little is fine, but delaying for months to get a few extra dollars isn't worth it.

Given how fast the world is moving, chasing the next big opportunity is the best risk/return move.
